## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 47, titled *Catumāsappaccayapavāraṇā* ("Accepting an invitation of more than four months"), is a monastic rule in the Theravāda Vinaya Piṭaka regulating how Buddhist monks accept invitations from lay supporters for requisites [SuttaCentral]. Under this training rule, a monk who exceeds the specific terms of an invitation when requesting requisites commits an expiation offense (*pācittiya*) [SuttaCentral]. In secondary analysis, Ute Hüsken notes this four-month provision (Pāc 47) in connection with the minimum duration monastics spend in a single dwelling place, under which a standing invitation for requisites is ordinarily valid for a period of only up to four months [Hüsken 1997]. Complete translations of the text include an English rendering by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
The rule is widely preserved across early Buddhist monastic lineages. Curated parallels on SuttaCentral record corresponding Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha and Vibhaṅga rules in the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahāsāṅghika, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, and Upāliparipṛcchā traditions, preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan [SuttaCentral]. Within the Pāli canon, it corresponds internally to the Pātimokkha rule, the Bhikkhu Parivāra, and the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (Pācittiya 128) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus computational analysis highlights extensive Pali-internal text reuse with various Khandhaka sections—particularly the Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka (Kd 15), Bhikkhunikkhandhaka (Kd 20), Senāsanakkhandhaka (Kd 16), and Bhesajjakkhandhaka (Kd 6)—as well as Nikāya discourses in the Sotāpatti Saṁyutta (SN 55), Aṭṭhakanipāta (AN 8), and Ekādasakanipāta (AN 11), along with subcommentaries like the *Vinayavinicchayaṭīkā* and *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇīpurāṇa-ṭīkā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns portions of the rule with Tibetan translations of canonical and commentarial Vinaya works, including the *Pratimokṣasūtrapaddhati* (D4104), *Vinayasaṃgraha* (D4105), and *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D0003-4) [DharmaNexus].
